claims.text: Slower thermal ramp rates and moderated peak temperatures promote formation of a uniform protective surface oxide on near-equiatomic, low-noble-metal solid-solution nanoparticles.
The resulting surface oxide is self-limiting or self-passivating.
A protective oxide layer mediates structural and chemical stability during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service.
The starting nanoparticles are nominally homogeneous solid solutions.
The starting nanoparticles have unresolved short- and long-range chemical order.
Relevant catalytic service temperatures are 773–1173 K, and relevant thermoelectric service temperatures are 473–1923 K.
Cr-, Al-, or Si-containing alloys can form chromia, alumina, or silica protective layers, respectively.
Compact protective oxide layers can inhibit further oxidation.
Chromia, alumina, and silica layers can act as diffusion barriers.
A slower treatment permits gradual oxidation that produces a coherent and uniform oxide film.
The oxide film limits elevated-temperature diffusion within the nanoparticles.
The oxide film suppresses phase separation or changes in chemical ordering inside the nanoparticles.
Rapid heating produces less uniform oxidation than slow heating.
Rapid heating enhances diffusion and accelerates nanoparticle destabilization.
Slow-treated nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation and fewer ordering changes than rapidly treated nanoparticles.
Slow-treated nanoparticles will have a more uniform and adherent oxide layer than rapidly treated nanoparticles.
The proposed effect requires a moderately oxidizing environment that permits controlled oxide formation.
The mechanism may not apply in highly reducing or excessively oxidizing environments or for substantially different compositions.

contradictions.description: The conditions include inert atmospheres, but the proposed mediator requires surface oxidation and the boundary restricts the expected effect to moderately oxidizing environments. The hypothesis therefore overextends the mechanism to a condition in which its required oxide may not form.
